extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners; patent applicants and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and rebutting obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103, including what prior art may be relied upon, how to treat analogous art, how to consider differences between the claimed invention and the prior art, and how to handle applicant rebuttal evidence and traverses.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.111(b) requirements for replies and traverses
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.111(b) requires applicant to distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable over any applied references. If an applicant disagrees with any factual findings by the Office, an effective traverse of a rejection based wholly or partially on such findings must include a reasoned statement explaining why the applicant believes the Office has erred substantively as to the factual findings. A mere statement or argument that the Office has not established a prima facie case of obviousness or that the Office’s reliance on common knowledge is unsupported by documentary evidence will not be considered substantively adequate. Office personnel may repeat the rejection made in the prior Office action and make the next Office action final. See MPEP § 706.07(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant's rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all rebuttal evidence that is timely presented by the applicants when reevaluating any obviousness determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence may include secondary considerations (e.g., commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others) and evidence of unexpected results. Applicants may submit evidence or argument showing: (A) one of ordinary skill could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods (e.g., technological difficulties); (B) the elements in combination do not merely perform the function that each element performs separately; or (C) the results of the claimed combination were unexpected. Once rebuttal evidence is presented, office personnel should reconsider initial determinations in view of the entire record, review all rejections and proposed rejections for continued viability, and clearly communicate findings and conclusions. Follow MPEP § 706.07(a), MPEP § 2145, and MPEP § 716–§ 716.10 regarding affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 and related procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 may be used for 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter that is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 can be used to support a rejection under section 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admitted prior art can be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations, regardless of whether it would otherwise qualify as prior art under statutory categories of 35 U.S.C. 102. A 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection is based on the specific statutory category applicable to the reference (e.g., 102(a)(1), (a)(2), pre-AIA categories). Publications that could be overcome by swearing behind the date may be addressed via affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.131. See MPEP § 901–§ 901.06(d), § 2121–§ 2129, and § 2151–§ 2155 for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive content requirements of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The substantive content of the prior art must be assessed for issues such as availability of inoperative devices, the extent to which prior art must be enabling, broad disclosure versus preferred embodiments, and admissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2121–§ 2129 for relevant case law and discussion about what prior art teaches and how enabling or broadly disclosed teachings are treated when relied upon in rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine prior art content as of the time the invention was made to avoid hindsight
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of the prior art is determined at the time the invention was made to avoid impermissible hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisionmakers must attempt to 'forget' what they have been taught about the claimed invention and cast the mind back to the time the invention was made, considering the perspective of one skilled in the art at that time. See MPEP § 2145 for discussion of rebutting applicant arguments that a rejection is based on hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — burden to establish applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 who wants to avail of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) bears the burden of establishing the conditions under which 103(c) applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish disqualification of certain prior art under 103(c), the applicant must show that the subject matter used in the rejection and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person. For joint research provisions (applications pending on or after December 10, 2004) the applicant must establish: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement. Note date limitations for pre-AIA provisions and see MPEP § 706.02(l)(1) and § 706.02(l)(2) for requirements to establish common ownership or joint research agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art requirement for reliance under 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on a reference in an obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference must be analogous prior art to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference is analogous art if: (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if it addresses a different problem); or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field). 'Reasonably pertinent' means the reference would have logically commended itself to an inventor's attention in considering the problem. The examiner should consider the problem faced by the inventor as reflected in the specification and may include a statement of the examiner's understanding of the problem to support pertinence. Applicant arguments that the examiner misconstrued the problem and relied on nonanalogous art should be fully considered in light of the specification. See KSR, In re Bigio, In re Icon Health and Fitness, In re Klein, and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of similarities and differences in structure and function
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining analogy, consider similarities and differences in structure and function, which often carry greater weight than classification or class-search cross-references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Office classification and class cross-references provide some evidence but courts emphasize structural and functional similarities/differences. Examiners should analyze these elements when determining whether a reference is reasonably pertinent or analogous (see In re Ellis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy considerations in the chemical arts
rubrics_metrics.description: In the chemical arts, references teaching similar chemical teachings (e.g., absorbing biologically active materials on carriers; dye chemistry) may be reasonably pertinent even if they originate in different specific product areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Ex parte Bland, Stratoflex, In re Mlot-Fijalkowski) show that if the problem is chemical in nature, teachings from related chemical fields are pertinent and may be analogous art because an inventor seeking solutions would look to those fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy considerations in the mechanical arts
rubrics_metrics.description: For simple mechanical inventions, a broad spectrum of prior art should be explored and it is reasonable to permit inquiry into other areas where one of ordinary skill would be aware that similar problems exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical examples (Stevenson v. ITC, In re Bigio, In re Deminski, Pentec, Ex parte Goodyear) show that structural similarity and shared problems across different device types can make references analogous art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy considerations in the electrical arts
rubrics_metrics.description: In electrical arts, solutions to similar functional problems in different devices or fields may be considered analogous art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one of ordinary skill in a given electrical art would look to solutions in other electrical or high-power, high-frequency devices for analogous rate-limiting or control problems, those references may be reasonably pertinent (see Medtronic v. Cardiac Pacemakers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy considerations in the design arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Design art analogy depends on whether prior designs are of the same general use as the claimed design or would reasonably fall within the knowledge of a designer of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and case law (MPEP § 1504.03, In re Rosen, Ex parte Pappas, In re Butera) illustrate that contemporary designs in related furniture or structural contexts may be analogous, while designs for unrelated uses (e.g., metal ball anode) may be nonanalogous if a designer would not have reason to look to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider differences between prior art and claimed invention 'as a whole'
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertaining differences requires interpreting claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art references as a whole; the question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not isolate or overweight individual differences; consider admitted unobvious aspects of components or steps in light of the entire claimed combination. Case examples (Stratoflex, In re Hirao) demonstrate that combinations of steps or integrated structures may render the invention nonobvious even if individual parts were known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not distill the invention to a 'gist' or 'thrust' that disregards 'as a whole' analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Distilling an invention down to the 'gist' or 'thrust' disregards the requirement to analyze the subject matter 'as a whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focusing only on a perceived advantage or single feature (e.g., a one-word solution or isolated limitation) can ignore express limitations and other claim elements and lead to improper obviousness conclusions. See W.L. Gore, Bausch & Lomb, Jones v. Hardy, Panduit for examples where such distillation was rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of the source or cause of a problem as part of the 'as a whole' inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovering the source or cause of a problem can be a patentable contribution even if the remedy would be obvious once the source is identified; this discovery is part of the subject matter 'as a whole' to be considered for obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, discovery of the cause does not always result in patentability if the solution would have been obvious from prior art that contains the same solution for a similar problem. Case law (In re Sponnoble; In re Wiseman) addresses when discovery supports nonobviousness versus when it does not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants alleging discovery must substantiate their allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants who allege they discovered the source of a problem must provide substantiating evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantiation may be by affidavits/declarations (e.g., under 37 CFR 1.132/1.131) or by a clear and persuasive assertion in the specification. Unsubstantiated statements of counsel are insufficient (see In re Wiseman, In re Kaslow).
